content: Information on the hazards and risks associated with various chemicals not covered in these guidelines can be obtained from multiple sources. These include the World Health Organization (WHO) Environmental Health Criteria monographs, Concise International Chemical Assessment Documents, reports from the Joint Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO)/WHO Meeting on Pesticide Residues, and the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives, as well as data from competent national authorities. These sources have undergone peer review and provide accessible information on the toxicology, hazards, and risks of less common contaminants. This information is valuable for water suppliers and health officials in assessing the significance of detected chemicals and determining appropriate responses. The development of drinking-water quality standards involves setting health-based targets, including numerical guideline values and other objectives outlined in the WHO Guidelines for Drinking-Water Quality. These targets are not intended to be mandatory limits but serve as scientific starting points for creating national or regional standards. Consequently, national standards may differ significantly from the guidelines in both scope and risk targets. A practical program with achievable goals, focusing on priority health concerns and attainable water quality levels, may yield better results than an overly ambitious one. Public health agencies, often closer to the community than water supply authorities, play a critical role in fostering community involvement. Supporting documents, such as those on developing drinking-water quality regulations, provide further guidance. Authorities are encouraged to develop context-specific guideline values tailored to local conditions. For example, in areas with high water consumption due to manual labor in hot climates, adjustments to daily water intake values may be necessary when setting local standards, such as for fluoride. Volatile substances in water may also pose inhalation risks during activities like showering, necessitating adjustments to guideline values for highly volatile chemicals like chloroform. Periodic review and revision of standards are crucial as knowledge evolves. Changes in guideline values, new hazards, advancements in water treatment technology, and shifts in public health risks or management capacity should be considered. National standards must be structured for easy updates, with modifications based on risk assessment and resource prioritization. Communication of justified changes to all stakeholders is essential. Drinking-water regulations should incorporate preventive risk management and prioritization approaches. Regulations should align with the principles outlined in the guidelines, ensuring safe drinking water from source to consumer through multiple barriers. They should be based on proven practices, supported by tools for compliance, and adaptable to changing contexts and technological innovations. Stakeholder roles and responsibilities must be clearly defined, and information sharing should be transparent and actionable. The ultimate goal of drinking-water quality regulations is to provide consumers with sustainable, sufficient, and safe drinking water. Regulations should focus on improving water safety through various tools and compliance strategies. While sanctions may be necessary, the primary aim is not to shut down deficient supplies but to encourage progressive improvements. These include providing adequate resources to regulatory authorities and assisting those required to comply with regulations. Health-based targets are measurable objectives established based on safety judgments and risk assessments of waterborne hazards. They are integral to existing drinking-water guidelines and serve as benchmarks for water suppliers and regulators to assess system adequacy or identify improvement needs. These targets support the development of water safety plans and incremental progress toward public health goals. They should be realistic, measurable, and relevant to local conditions, considering economic, environmental, social, and cultural factors. The concept of a tolerable burden of disease, expressed in disability-adjusted life years (DALYs), provides a common metric for quantifying and comparing the health impacts of various water-related hazards. The WHO defines a tolerable disease burden as an upper limit of 10⁻⁶ DALY per person per year, equivalent to one excess case of cancer per 100,000 people over a 70-year period. This metric enables consistent risk assessment across microbial, chemical, and radiological hazards. However, achieving this target may not be feasible in some locations, and less stringent interim targets may be necessary to encourage incremental improvements. Health-based targets should account for short-term events and fluctuations in water quality, such as those caused by heavy rain or maintenance activities. The multiple-barrier principle remains critical for water safety, especially during catastrophic events that degrade source water quality or lead to system failures. Performance targets, expressed as percentage removals or specified technology requirements, can also be applied to chemical hazards. For microbial hazards, health-based targets often take the form of performance or specified technology targets, as monitoring finished drinking water for pathogens is not cost-effective. Instead, indicator organisms like E. coli are monitored. Risks to public health are typically attributed to single hazards, and reference risk levels are applied independently to each hazard. Health outcome targets, such as limits on diarrheal disease or cancer incidence, represent tolerable disease burdens and are typically set at the national level. These targets must be translated into actionable water quality, performance, or technology targets for water suppliers as part of water safety plans. Incremental progress toward these targets can be supported by setting milestones and using health-based targets to guide improvements in water quality and public health.
